The Risk We Buried · Everything Is On Track, Book 3

Chapter 1

About 15 minutes of reading.

Agnes Pryor had put the bank statements in date order and the cookies in a measuring cup.

“The lid broke,” she said when Lena looked at it. “On the tin. There’s nothing wrong with the cookies.”

She tipped the cup and shook two onto a plate. One landed on its edge, rolled into the other and broke.

“They were whole this morning.”

Lena took the broken one.

She had been on the Monday bus since a quarter to eight, two changes and a long walk past the freight yards. The car had gone in the spring. She had not missed it as much as she had expected, and on the second bus she had read the client’s email again with nothing to do but read it.

The office overlooked the warehouse through a window reinforced with wire. Below it, a woman was stretching clear film around a stack of cartons, walking backward with a confidence Lena found difficult to watch. Each circuit pulled the loose boxes closer together.

Agnes moved a ledger off the spare chair.

“I thought you’d want paper. My accountant always wanted paper.”

“Electronic copies will help too.”

“Oh, I’ve got those. This is so I can find what you’re asking about.”

She sat opposite Lena. Her cardigan had a shiny patch at one elbow, and she had written three figures on the back of her left hand. Two were crossed out.

“Merebank Stores,” she began, then stopped. “You know where you are.”

“I know you’re member-owned. Businesses rent storage here.”

“We own the co-op. The building we lease, which is a sentence I say a lot. And it’s mostly businesses. We’ve got a theater group in bay nineteen. They’d object to being called a business right up until you offered them the business rate.”

Agnes smiled, waiting to see whether Lena would. Then she opened the folder between them.

“I’m the treasurer. Volunteer. I also run this office three days a week, which nobody ever voted for. We need the emergency reserve reconciled before the renewal notices go out.”

“Which period?”

“The year through the end of last month. We renew the storage agreements together, even when people joined halfway through. It saves having different terms going around.”

She pushed across a sheet headed RESERVE SUMMARY. A figure at the bottom had been underlined hard enough to shine.

“That’s what I make it. I’d like someone else to make it the same.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Then I’d like to know where I’ve gone wrong.”

Agnes said it readily enough. Lena went down the sheet. There were monthly contributions, bank interest, two payments, a line reversed, and a transfer described only as adjustment.

“Does the reserve have its own bank account?”

“Yes. Although things have occasionally gone through the checking account first. People use the saved payment details.”

“Contributions from members?”

“Part of their monthly charge. It’s broken out on the invoice.”

“Can I have those invoices, the ledger and the statements for both accounts?”

Agnes drew a second folder from beneath the first.

“I was hoping you’d say that. I spent Sunday downloading them.”

“Before we go further,” Lena said, “what do you need to be able to tell the members?”

“That the figure is right.”

“Where will they see it?”

“In the annual accounts eventually. For now, with their renewals.”

Agnes took a thin bundle held together with a black clip. She took off the clip, flattened the pages and found the covering letter.

Lena read the paragraph Agnes indicated.

The emergency reserve continued to provide security for members and their businesses. The balance would be confirmed following an independent check.

“Who wrote this?”

“I did.”

“Has it gone out?”

“No. I haven’t even bought the envelopes.”

Lena read it again. Downstairs, the woman had finished wrapping the cartons. She pressed the end of the film against one corner with the flat of her hand.

“What does the reserve pay for?”

“Emergencies affecting the building. Urgent repairs. Keeping things going if we have to close part of it.”

“Members’ losses?”

“They insure their own stock.”

“Does everyone understand that?”

Agnes put the renewal letter down.

“This is bookkeeping, Lena. I’m not asking you to review all our arrangements.”

“I understand. I need the letter to describe the bookkeeping.”

Agnes did not move. Then she picked up her pen.

“Show me.”

Lena turned the page toward her.

“Confirming how much money is recorded, and whether we can account for it, won’t tell us how far it would go in an emergency.”

“We’ve never claimed it covers everything.”

“This sentence doesn’t say what it covers.”

Agnes tapped the word security once with her pen. The point left a blue dot beneath it.

“We’re trying to get people to renew. Rates have gone up, and they’re already annoyed about paying more for the same concrete floor. I don’t want a letter that sounds as if we expect the roof to come off.”

“Neither do I.”

“What would you put?”

“Tell them what the reserve is for. Give the balance and the date. Say the reconciliation is being done.”

“Being done, or completed?”

“Whichever is true when you send it.”

Agnes pulled the letter back and crossed out the paragraph. She wrote in the margin, slowly, moving the cookie plate when her hand reached it.

Lena opened her laptop.

“I’ll put the same distinction in my engagement letter.”

“How much distinction?”

“A deliverable we can both point to.”

The screen woke to the draft Lena had prepared from Agnes’s email. She changed the description of the work, then turned the laptop so they could read together.

A reconciliation of the emergency reserve ledger to the bank balances at the period end. A schedule of transfers, receipts and payments, with supporting records referenced. A separate list of differences and items for which records were missing.

Agnes leaned forward.

“Will you correct the ledger?”

“I can propose entries. You approve them and whoever maintains it posts them. I’ll show the balance before and after.”

“That’s me, mostly.”

“Then I’ll send them to you.”

“And how long?”

“Three working days once I have the records. If something’s missing, I’ll identify it. I won’t keep extending the job while we wait.”

“Good. I can follow up a missing receipt. I can’t hold back sixty-three renewal notices forever.”

Lena added a paragraph beneath the deliverables. The work would not assess the adequacy of the reserve, insurance cover, the condition of the premises or protection available to individual members.

This was her third contract since she had left the bank, and every letter had a paragraph like this one. She kept the jobs small on purpose. If a job needed to grow, someone would have to ask her, in writing, before it did. She had once been the person who said yes to everything in the room, and she remembered what that had cost other people.

Agnes read it without speaking.

“Do you need the rules?” she asked at last.

“Yes. Anything governing contributions or permitted spending. And the decisions authorizing the payments.”

“I thought you weren’t reviewing the protection.”

“I’m not. But I need to know what each payment was recorded against. If I can’t show that, it goes on the list.”

Agnes reached down beside her chair and brought up a green binder.

“The minutes are here. Some attachments are in email. I can get you those.”

Lena added them to the records requested. Under access, she specified copies of the relevant accounting records and decisions. No authority to move money or approve expenditure.

“Wouldn’t give you the bank password anyway,” Agnes said.

“Good.”

“My husband thinks writing it backward makes it safe.”

“Does he?”

“He doesn’t have ours.”

Agnes grinned, then bent over the screen again. She read every line this time, following one with her finger held just above the glass.

“Differences reported even if they’re small?”

“Even if they’re small.”

“All right.”

Lena emailed the letter across. Agnes’s computer sounded behind her. She turned, opened it and found the signature field, taking off her glasses to inspect the date before putting them back on.

When the signed copy arrived, Lena saved it and closed the draft.

Agnes gathered the statements. Beneath them lay the renewal letter with its crossed-out paragraph, and under that a short stack of printed forms. She lifted the letter clear before sliding the folder over.

“I’ll finish this after we’ve looked around,” she said. “You can tell me if I’ve described your bit properly.”

“I will.”

Agnes put the letter beside her keyboard, where she would have to move it to type, and stood.

“Bring your coat. It’s colder down there.”

The stairs came out beside a cage of empty gas cylinders. Agnes waited while Lena put on her coat, then pulled the door shut until the latch caught.

“Office heat goes straight up there if you let it.”

On the warehouse floor, the cold reached through Lena’s shoes. White lines divided the concrete into bays. Some held shelving and labeled cartons; others contained objects she could not identify beneath old blankets. Above one partition hung a painted moon with a bite missing from its edge.

“The theater,” Agnes said. “They promise that’s the last big thing until February.”

A man in a dark fleece came toward them carrying a clipboard. Before Agnes could introduce him, someone called from the loading doors.

“Rafe. He’s leaving it here.”

The man turned.

“No, he isn’t.”

Beyond him, a delivery driver was lowering the liftgate of a truck. On it stood a long wooden crate, strapped to a pallet that extended past both ends. A younger man in a wool hat waited with a delivery slip in his hand.

“Sorry,” Rafe said to Lena. “Give me a minute.”

He walked quickly without running. Agnes followed, and Lena went with her, stopping inside the yellow line that crossed the floor before the doors.

“You can’t put that in the lane,” Rafe told the driver.

“Curbside delivery.”

“This isn’t the curb.”

“It’s where he told me.”

The younger man raised the slip a little.

“I said outside my bay.”

“Your bay’s around the corner, Wes.”

“I know. He said he couldn’t get around.”

The driver pressed the control. The liftgate went down another few inches, then stopped.

“I’ve got four drops after this.”

Rafe looked along the lane. A woman stood behind a cart of brown paper sacks, watching them. She had already taken her gloves off and tucked them under one arm.

“Keep it on the gate,” Rafe said. “I’ll get the long jack.”

“Is he signing?”

“When we’ve got it down safely.”

Rafe pointed Wes toward the sacks.

“Ask Mo to hold there. Then clear whatever you’ve got outside sixteen.”

“It’s only the trestles.”

“Clear the trestles.”

Wes put the delivery slip between his teeth and went.

“This is Rafe Ward,” Agnes said as Rafe passed them. “He manages the place.”

“Usually I make people tea,” he said. “Today you get this.”

He disappeared between two rows of shelving.

Wes had reached his bay. He lifted a pair of folded trestles against his chest, turned, found his way blocked by a stool and put them down again.

“Don’t watch,” Agnes murmured.

Lena looked away. On the wall beside her was a board headed EQUIPMENT OUT. Names and times had been written against a platform cart, a carpet cleaner, two hand trucks and something called the blue beast. Beside LONG PALLET JACK someone had written BACK, LEFT BY CUTTING TABLE.

Rafe returned pulling it behind him.

“Found it?” Agnes asked.

“Exactly where the board said. A historic morning.”

He stopped at the yellow line.

“Could you stay this side, please?”

“Of course.”

The driver lowered the gate to the floor. Rafe crouched to check beneath the pallet, then worked the forks into place. Wes came back without the slip in his mouth.

“What is it?” Agnes asked him.

“Tabletop. Ash. Customer wanted it in one piece.”

“Must have a big dining room.”

“She hasn’t got the house yet.”

Agnes looked at him.

“She’s under contract,” he added. “I took a deposit.”

Rafe pumped the handle. The crate rose, and the driver stepped off the gate with the expression of a man whose part was finished.

“Wes, watch the back corner. Don’t put your hand between it and anything.”

They brought it forward slowly. One wheel clicked at every turn. At the corner, Wes said, “Stop,” too quietly, then said it again, loudly enough.

Rafe stopped.

A strip of packing timber stuck out from the crate. It would not clear the steel upright.

“We can take that off,” Wes said.

“Or we can go wider.”

They went wider. Lena moved back until her coat touched the wall. The crate passed with room to spare.

Mo waited by her cart. When the lane cleared, she put her gloves on again.

“About time. My flour’s getting older.”

“Send me the bill,” Rafe said.

“I do. Every month.”

She pushed past him toward the doors.

Agnes led Lena after the crate. Inside bay sixteen, a workbench ran beneath shelves of timber offcuts. A chair without a seat hung from a hook, its front legs polished darker than the rest.

Rafe lowered the pallet onto two wooden blocks and pulled the jack free.

“Don’t unpack into the lane.”

“I won’t.”

“You said that about the wardrobe.”

“That was because of the mirror.”

Rafe waited.

“I won’t,” Wes said again.

While Wes signed the driver’s terminal, a woman in a green apron came around the partition carrying a sample book.

“Is that the table for the woman on West Street? What height are you making the seats?”

“Eighteen inches finished.”

“Including my cushion?”

He hesitated.

She opened the sample book against the crate.

“Come and measure one before you cut anything.”

“Upholstery,” Agnes said to Lena, as the two of them went off arguing about inches. “Bay twelve. He sent her a customer, she sent him one. It goes back and forth.”

Rafe parked the pallet jack in a marked rectangle beside the equipment board. He erased the note about the cutting table and hung the pen back on its string.

“Does everyone have their own handling equipment?” Lena asked.

“Some do. The long jack belongs to the co-op. No point having twelve things nobody’s got room to turn.”

“And people help with deliveries?”

“When they can. We try to book anything awkward.” He looked toward sixteen. “Sometimes awkward arrives early.”

Agnes took Lena down the next aisle. A handwritten notice offered spare space in a refrigerated van on Thursdays. Beneath it, someone wanted a person to cover two market mornings. Three phone-number tabs had been torn away.

Near the end of the aisle a woman knelt on the concrete with a tape measure, running it across an empty patch of floor at the front of her bay. A roll of brown tape hung on her wrist like a bracelet. Behind her, cartons were stacked to the shelf tops.

“Farah,” Agnes said. “Packaging. She’s measuring for something that hasn’t come yet.”

“It comes flat,” Farah said, without looking up. “Everyone says that as if it helps.”

She let the tape snap back and wrote a number on the back of her hand. Lena saw that it joined two others already there.

“Where would Wes work if he left here?” Lena asked when they had turned the corner.

“His garage, perhaps. He started there.”

“Could he get that tabletop in?”

Agnes looked back along the aisle.

“No. I don’t suppose he could.”

Through a gap in the shelving, the upholsterer was holding a tape measure while Wes sat on a padded bench. He started to stand; she pushed his shoulder down and read the measurement again.

Lena had seen the monthly storage charges upstairs. She had a rough idea now of what another building might cost. She could not put a figure against finding an upholsterer nearby, or having someone stop cutting a seat to help move a crate.

“Have I shown you enough concrete floor?” Agnes asked.

“Plenty.”

“Back up, then. You’ll want those electronic records.”

At the stairs they met Mo returning with the empty cart.

“Agnes, are the renewals coming this week?”

“That’s the intention.”

“Today would be better. I need to book my year-end stock, and the mill wants an answer by Friday.”

“Then today’s the intention.”

Mo lifted the cart’s front wheels over the door sill and carried on.

Upstairs, the office window had misted at one corner. The corrected renewal letter lay beside the keyboard, and Lena’s folder waited on the spare chair.

She took off her coat and sat down.

“Got it?”

The man was in the doorway before Lena had got past the list of files. He carried a padded envelope and a pair of work gloves, and he had a red mark across one cheek where his hat had pressed against it. He did not knock. He had the look of someone who had rehearsed the conversation on the stairs and won it.

Agnes opened a drawer. A key on a yellow plastic tag lay in a small paper bag.

“Came yesterday. Twelve dollars, please.”

He stopped folding his gloves.

“You said you’d take care of it.”

“I have. It took an extra day because they didn’t have the blank.”

“The charge, Agnes. I lent mine to the people collecting from bay eight, when their driver couldn’t get back in. You told me to. They took it away with them. So I’m not paying twelve dollars for helping you.”

Agnes kept the paper bag in her hand.

“I asked whether you could let them use yours. I didn’t know they were going to take it.”

“Neither did I.”

Lena turned her chair slightly.

“If there’s an entry you need traced, I can look while Agnes finds the instruction.”

Agnes passed her a narrow hardback book with KEYS written along the spine. Lena opened it at the ribbon. In Agnes’s handwriting was an order for a replacement, with the member number, the date and twelve dollars in the cost column. The column beside it was headed COLLECTED. It was empty.

“Has this gone onto his account?”

“I do the extras on Friday. I was waiting for him to collect it.”

“Then there isn’t a charge to trace yet,” Lena said. “This needs a decision about the fee, not a correction.”

He laid his gloves on the envelope.

“A favor, you mean.”

“No.”

“Because I’ve already done one. I’m standing here asking for twelve dollars off. That’s what it sounds like.”

Lena closed the book, leaving her finger between the pages.

“That came out wrong. I offered to find a mistake, and there isn’t one written down. You’re not the problem.”

He looked at Agnes.

“Can I get into my bay or not?”

“Yes.”

“And then get a bill?”

“I need to check who can agree to remove the fee.”

“You asked me to give them the key.”

“I did.” Agnes put the empty paper bag on the desk. “And when you called, I said I’d take care of it. I meant I’d get another key made. I didn’t tell you I meant only that.”

“You could have mentioned the twelve dollars.”

She flattened the bag with her palm. The torn corner folded underneath.

“I should have.”

He rubbed a thumb along the seam of his gloves.

“I’m issuing the key now,” Agnes said. “I’ll record the twelve dollars as outstanding, with a note that you dispute it and I’m taking it to the chair. You don’t have to pay it to take the key.”

“And you’ll say why?”

“Yes.”

She wrote slowly, then turned the book toward him.

“You asked me to lend it,” he said. “Can you put that? Not just that I lent it.”

Agnes added the words above the line and initialed them. He read the entry again, signed for collection and put the key in his pocket.

“I’ll call those people again,” he said. “Might still be in their van.”

After he had gone, Agnes copied the disputed-fee note onto her list of extras. She checked both versions before she closed the book.

Lena opened the reserve file. She had offered that small certainty, a payment found or a reference matched, before asking whether there was anything for it to attach to. She noticed it, and did not like it.

Agnes was squaring the stack of printed forms she had lifted from under the renewal letter. The top one had a member’s bay number, the coming year’s charges in a table and, below the table, a box on its own with a great deal of white space around it.

PROTECTED STOCK VALUE.

Beneath it stood a single amount.

“Is that part of the renewal pack?” Lena asked.

“Letter and statement together. They go out this afternoon. Email for most, envelopes for six, if I find envelopes. Why?”

Lena read the heading again. Protected by what, and up to how much, the form did not say. It was not in her letter. Her letter was the ledger.

“No reason yet,” she said.

She wrote the heading on a sticky note, pressed it to the frame of her screen where she would see it every time she looked up, and opened the ledger.

A measuring cup of cookies, a reserve to reconcile. Now the work begins.
